opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the most interesting questions with these depth-recurrent models, because the whole point is that you can spend more or less compute depending on how hard a token or a problem is. In our recurrent-depth model, the architecture has a prelude that embeds the input into a latent space, a core block that we iterate on that latent state, and then a coda that decodes back out. At training time we sample a random number of iterations, so the model learns to work across a range of compute budgets. At test time, though, you have to decide when to stop.

The simplest thing is a fixed budget: say, run 32 iterations for everything. That works, but it's wasteful, because a lot of tokens are easy. If you're just finishing a word or emitting punctuation, the model converges almost immediately.

So what we've looked at are adaptive exit criteria that don't need any extra training. The one I like is to watch how much the model's output distribution is still changing from one iteration to the next. You compute something like the KL divergence between the next-token distribution at step k and step k minus one, and once it falls below a threshold you've basically converged and can exit. You can also look at the norm of the change in the latent state, which is cheaper. Both work reasonably well, and the nice thing is they're zero-shot. The model was never explicitly trained to exit early, but because it learned to converge toward a stable state, these signals fall out naturally.

When you do this, you see really intuitive behavior. The model spends very few iterations on easy continuations and many more on, say, a step in a math problem where it actually has to compute something. Different domains end up with visibly different average compute.

There are subtleties. The threshold is a knob that trades accuracy against compute, and it isn't universal across tasks. You also need to handle the KV cache sensibly, since tokens exit at different depths. You can reuse the cache from the last computed iteration, or share cache entries across depths, and the model turns out to be surprisingly robust to that. You also have to make sure convergence actually means "done" and not "stuck." Sometimes the latent state settles into orbits or slow drifts instead of a fixed point, so you want a criterion that isn't fooled by that.

Longer term, I think the interesting direction is learning the stopping policy, or having the model signal its own confidence, without losing the nice property that the core model is trained cleanly and you get adaptivity almost for free. But the empirical observation that simple convergence checks already work is, I think, one of the more encouraging things about this whole approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the questions that I find most interesting about the whole recurrent-depth setup, because the stopping criterion is where a lot of the elegance either shows up or falls apart.

The way we think about it is that the model has this recurrent block that you can just keep applying to the latent state. During training, we sample the number of recurrences from a distribution, something like a log-normal Poisson, so the model sees anything from one or two iterations up to thirty-two or more, and it learns to make progress at every step rather than only producing a good answer at some fixed depth. That's the key property. Because of that, at inference time you have freedom in how you choose the depth, and the question becomes: what signal do you actually use to stop?

The simplest thing, and honestly what we use for most evaluations, is just a fixed budget. You say, I'll give it thirty-two steps, or sixty-four, and you stop. That's boring but it's predictable, and it's what you want for benchmarking because it makes comparisons clean.

The more interesting thing is adaptive stopping, and there the natural signal is convergence of the latent state itself. You look at how much the hidden state is still changing between iteration t and t plus one, and when that difference drops below some threshold, you stop. What's nice is that this is zero-shot, you don't have to train a separate halting head or build in any kind of learned stopping mechanism the way earlier adaptive-compute work did. The model just converges, because it was trained to behave like an iterative refinement process, and you read that convergence off the states directly. And what we observed is that different tokens converge at very different rates. Some tokens settle in a handful of steps, others keep moving for a long time, and those tend to be the ones where there's real computation happening, so you get this emergent per-token compute allocation almost for free.

There's a second option that's a bit more output-focused, which is to look at the KL divergence between the output distribution at successive steps, so you're asking whether the model's prediction has stabilized rather than whether the internal state has. In practice those two track each other fairly closely, but the KL-based one is slightly more aligned with what you actually care about.

The caveat I'd give is that convergence isn't the same thing as correctness. The state can settle on a wrong answer. So the stopping rule is really about not wasting compute once the model has made up its mind, not a guarantee that more iterations wouldn't have helped on some different trajectory. And there are some subtleties around the KV cache, because if you're stopping at different depths for different tokens, you have to decide which iteration's cache entries later tokens should attend to. We found that just sharing the cache across a window of recent steps works reasonably well, but it's one of those details that I think deserves more careful study than we've given it so far.

r003.rationale: It describes stopping when the latent state’s change between successive recurrences falls below a threshold, and says this requires no separate learned stopping mechanism.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two questions here: how much computation do you want to spend, and how do you know whether another iteration will actually help? The simplest approach is to set a budget. You run a fixed number of recurrent steps, and you can vary that number depending on your latency constraints.

But ideally, the model would decide dynamically. One signal you can look at is whether its state, or its prediction for the next token, is still changing. If the output distribution is essentially the same over successive iterations, that’s a reasonable indication that you could stop. The tricky part is that stability doesn’t necessarily mean correctness. The model can settle on a wrong answer, and a small change in the hidden state might still matter downstream.

So I’d treat convergence as a useful heuristic, rather than a complete solution. What you really want is a stopping mechanism that learns whether the expected benefit of another step is worth its computational cost. And that decision could be different for every token—you don’t necessarily need the same amount of computation everywhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as an adaptive computation problem. For a given token, you can run the recurrent block a few times and ask whether another iteration is still changing the prediction in a meaningful way. If the output distribution has stabilized, that’s a reasonable signal to stop. If it’s still changing, you might want to spend more compute.

The tricky part is that stability doesn’t necessarily mean correctness. The model can settle on a wrong answer, and an intermediate prediction can look confident before further computation changes it. So you want to evaluate the stopping rule against the actual benefit of additional iterations, rather than relying on confidence alone.

A fixed iteration budget is a useful baseline. From there, the goal is to learn or design a stopping criterion that allocates more computation where it helps, while accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop.
